title: Weighing Molecules to Name Them
endLine: Weighing charged ions and fragments identifies molecules and reads protein sequences.

scenes.tts: A cell holds thousands of proteins, so how do you identify one? An enzyme assay tracks activity, and a gel sorts proteins by size. Neither names the molecule or reads its amino acid sequence. Mass spectrometry answers by weighing molecules.
scenes.caption: A cell holds thousands of proteins, so how do you identify one? An enzyme assay tracks activity, and a gel sorts proteins by size. Neither names the molecule or reads its amino acid sequence. Mass spectrometry answers by weighing molecules.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Open full-frame on a glowing sample tube filled with drifting colored spheres representing thousands of proteins; one gold sphere pulses with a bold question mark before the narrator asks how to identify one. As activity is named, a rising gauge briefly ticks beside the tube; as gel sorting is named, bands slide downward by length on a compact strip while the question mark stays over the gold band. The strip dissolves smoothly into the left inlet of a wide horizontal mass spectrometer bench (inlet, ionizer, analyzer chamber, detector screen, filling most of the frame height) as the gold sphere drifts toward the inlet.
scenes.narration: A cell holds thousands of proteins, so how do you identify one? An enzyme assay tracks activity, and a gel sorts proteins by size. Neither names the molecule or reads its amino acid sequence. Mass spectrometry answers by weighing molecules.

scenes.visual: Schematic. The horizontal mass spectrometer bench holds softly lit in the background with spheres drifting slowly into the left inlet while the title 'Weighing Molecules to Name Them' fades in clean and large across center, holds briefly, then clears as the bench brightens.

scenes.tts: Neutral molecules ignore electric fields, so the instrument first adds a charge to make ions. More charge brings a stronger push, while more mass resists it. The analyzer sorts ions by mass divided by charge, the mass-to-charge ratio. Each ratio produces a peak.
scenes.caption: Neutral molecules ignore electric fields, so the instrument first adds a charge to make ions. More charge brings a stronger push, while more mass resists it. The analyzer sorts ions by mass divided by charge, the mass-to-charge ratio. Each ratio produces a peak.
scenes.visual: Schematic (no molecular structures). On the carried bench, uncharged grey spheres drift straight past pulsing electric field plates without deflecting. In the ionizer, crisp '+' badges attach to spheres first, then the label 'Ions' appears as electric field arrows bend their paths: a double-charged small sphere accelerates strongly while a heavier single-charged sphere turns slowly. The formula 'mass / charge' appears above the analyzer chamber as ions separate into distinct streams, landing on the right detector screen where vertical peaks rise in real time (labelled 'Schematic spectrum').
scenes.narration: Neutral molecules ignore electric fields, so the instrument first adds a charge to make ions. More charge brings a stronger push, while more mass resists it. The analyzer sorts ions by mass divided by charge, the mass-to-charge ratio. Each ratio produces a peak.

scenes.tts: One peak is a clue, not always a name. Suppose two different molecules share the same mass and charge. Both land on the same peak. How can a mass spectrometer still tell them apart?
scenes.caption: One peak is a clue, not always a name. Suppose two different molecules share the same mass and charge. Both land on the same peak. How can a mass spectrometer still tell them apart?
scenes.visual: Schematic (no molecular structures). Camera pushes gently into the analyzer and detector on the same bench. Two differently shaped colored icons — a teal hexagon and an amber diamond, both with the same mass label and '+' charge — travel side by side through the analyzer and stack onto a single glowing detector peak. A question card fades in cleanly above the spectrum: 'Same peak — how to tell them apart?'
scenes.narration: One peak is a clue, not always a name. Suppose two different molecules share the same mass and charge. Both land on the same peak. How can a mass spectrometer still tell them apart?

scenes.visual: Schematic. Hold the question 'Same peak — how to tell them apart?' cleanly above the detector while the teal hexagon and amber diamond pulse gently together on the shared peak and a slim timer bar glides smoothly along the bottom edge.

scenes.tts: Break them apart and weigh the pieces. In tandem mass spectrometry, the first stage isolates that peak and shatters its ions. Different molecules usually split into different fragments, which a second stage weighs. Weighing charged ions and fragments identifies molecules and reads protein sequences.
scenes.caption: Break them apart and weigh the pieces. In tandem mass spectrometry, the first stage isolates that peak and shatters its ions. Different molecules usually split into different fragments, which a second stage weighs. Weighing charged ions and fragments identifies molecules and reads protein sequences.
scenes.visual: Schematic (no molecular structures). The question clears and the analyzer expands along the same bench to reveal two stages bridged by a glowing collision cell. Stage 1 gates out all other ions and passes only the shared peak into the collision cell, where the teal hexagon splits into three small teal shards and the amber diamond splits into two uneven amber shards. Stage 2 sorts those shards into two distinct, non-overlapping peak patterns on the right detector (labelled 'Schematic fragment spectra') as the label 'Tandem MS' settles above.
scenes.narration: Break them apart and weigh the pieces. In tandem mass spectrometry, the first stage isolates that peak and shatters its ions. Different molecules usually split into different fragments, which a second stage weighs. Weighing charged ions and fragments identifies molecules and reads protein sequences.

scenes.tts: To sequence a protein, the enzyme trypsin first cuts it into short peptides. The first stage selects one peptide ion and breaks it into a ladder of fragments, each one amino acid shorter. Subtracting neighbouring masses names each amino acid in order. Two amino acids weigh exactly the same, though.
scenes.caption: To sequence a protein, the enzyme trypsin first cuts it into short peptides. The first stage selects one peptide ion and breaks it into a ladder of fragments, each one amino acid shorter. Subtracting neighbouring masses names each amino acid in order. Two amino acids weigh exactly the same, though.
scenes.visual: Schematic (no molecular structures). At the bench inlet, a long chain of colored beads (representing a protein) is snipped by a moving scissor icon labelled 'Trypsin' into short bead segments ('Peptides'). One four-bead peptide enters Stage 1, passes into the collision cell, and breaks into nested fragments of 4, 3, 2, and 1 beads. On the schematic detector spectrum, four peaks appear left to right; brackets animate between consecutive peaks with the formula 'mass gap = one amino acid's mass', and each bead color pops into place in sequence above the gaps; two beads of identical mass but different colour then flash together with the label 'Same mass'.
scenes.narration: To sequence a protein, the enzyme trypsin first cuts it into short peptides. The first stage selects one peptide ion and breaks it into a ladder of fragments, each one amino acid shorter. Subtracting neighbouring masses names each amino acid in order. Two amino acids weigh exactly the same, though.

scenes.tts: Crowded samples can hide scarce targets. Fasting blood holds insulin at a few tens of picomolar. Albumin outnumbers it roughly ten million to one, enough to drown its signal. So liquid chromatography separates the mixture first, feeding compounds in over time.
scenes.caption: Crowded samples can hide scarce targets. Fasting blood holds insulin at a few tens of picomolar. Albumin outnumbers it roughly ten million to one, enough to drown its signal. So liquid chromatography separates the mixture first, feeding compounds in over time.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Pan left on the same bench to the inlet: a dense cloud of grey spheres labelled 'Albumin' crowds around a single bright gold sphere labelled 'Insulin', with the ratio 'ten million to one' appearing clearly. When the crowded cloud enters the ionizer at once, the schematic detector floods with one towering grey spike burying the gold signal. A slim vertical tube labelled 'Liquid chromatography' slides into place before the inlet; grey and gold spheres now travel through the tube at different speeds and enter the ionizer sequentially, letting the gold peak rise cleanly on its own.
scenes.narration: Crowded samples can hide scarce targets. Fasting blood holds insulin at a few tens of picomolar. Albumin outnumbers it roughly ten million to one, enough to drown its signal. So liquid chromatography separates the mixture first, feeding compounds in over time.

scenes.tts: A missing peak needs caution. Every instrument has a detection limit, the lowest level it can reliably see. Not detected means below that floor, not zero, so studies report their limits. Strong claims also check whether two methods that fail differently agree.
scenes.caption: A missing peak needs caution. Every instrument has a detection limit, the lowest level it can reliably see. Not detected means below that floor, not zero, so studies report their limits. Strong claims also check whether two methods that fail differently agree.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Focus on the detector screen of the carried bench: a bright dashed horizontal line labelled 'Detection limit' sweeps across the baseline. A tiny amber peak pulses faintly underneath the dashed line, fading into noise as the label 'Below limit, not zero' settles beside it. On the lower edge, a second independent schematic gauge slides in beside the mass spectrum and both indicators light up together in agreement.
scenes.narration: A missing peak needs caution. Every instrument has a detection limit, the lowest level it can reliably see. Not detected means below that floor, not zero, so studies report their limits. Strong claims also check whether two methods that fail differently agree.

scenes.tts: The same care tracks drugs. Male mice received the drug isoguvacine, twenty milligrams per kilogram. Liquid chromatography mass spectrometry then detected it in blood and liver. It was not detected in brain or cerebrospinal fluid. Detection limits were six hundred forty picomolar in fluids and sixteen nanomolar in tissue.
scenes.caption: The same care tracks drugs. Male mice received the drug isoguvacine, 20 mg/kg. Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry then detected it in blood and liver. It was not detected in brain or cerebrospinal fluid. Detection limits were 640 picomolar in fluids and 16 nanomolar in tissue.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Keeping the liquid chromatography column and detector screen visible on the bench, four compact sample vials labelled 'Blood', 'Liver', 'Brain', and 'Cerebrospinal fluid' feed sequentially into the inlet. For 'Blood' and 'Liver', clear gold peaks rise well above the dashed detection-limit line; for 'Brain' and 'Cerebrospinal fluid', the trace stays flat below the floor while the exact numeric thresholds '640 picomolar (fluids)' and '16 nanomolar (tissue)' appear cleanly beside the line.
scenes.narration: The same care tracks drugs. Male mice received the drug isoguvacine, 20 mg/kg. Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry then detected it in blood and liver. It was not detected in brain or cerebrospinal fluid. Detection limits were 640 picomolar in fluids and 16 nanomolar in tissue.

scenes.tts: Tandem mass spectrometry also serves newborn screening. M C A D deficiency, a missing fat-burning enzyme, affects roughly one in ten thousand to twenty thousand births. A heel prick read by tandem mass spectrometry catches most cases. A few babies still fall ill before the result is back.
scenes.caption: Tandem mass spectrometry also serves newborn screening. MCAD deficiency, a missing fat-burning enzyme, affects roughly 1 in 10,000 to 20,000 births. A heel prick read by tandem mass spectrometry catches most cases. A few babies still fall ill before the result is back.
scenes.visual: Schematic. A single bright drop icon labelled 'Newborn heel prick' enters the tandem MS bench inlet; the label '1 in 10,000–20,000 births' appears gently beside it. Ions split through Stage 1 and Stage 2 into a crisp flagged marker peak labelled 'Flags MCAD deficiency (schematic)' on the schematic detector while a small clock icon ticks gently to mark the urgency before results return.
scenes.narration: Tandem mass spectrometry also serves newborn screening. MCAD deficiency, a missing fat-burning enzyme, affects roughly 1 in 10,000 to 20,000 births. A heel prick read by tandem mass spectrometry catches most cases. A few babies still fall ill before the result is back.

scenes.tts: Heavy nitrogen weighs more than normal nitrogen, so weighing tracks it. In the nineteen thirties, Rudolf Schoenheimer fed rats nitrogen-labeled amino acids. The heavy tag entered proteins throughout the body, showing the dynamic state of body constituents. Ion and fragment mass turns hidden mixtures into names and sequences.
scenes.caption: Heavy nitrogen weighs more than normal nitrogen, so weighing tracks it. In the 1930s, Rudolf Schoenheimer fed rats nitrogen-labeled amino acids. The heavy tag entered proteins throughout the body, showing "the dynamic state of body constituents." Ion and fragment mass turns hidden mixtures into names and sequences.
scenes.visual: Schematic. On the carried bench, a small bright-ringed heavy bead labelled 'Heavy nitrogen tag' (with 'Schoenheimer, 1930s') enters growing bead chains representing body proteins, shifting a schematic peak slightly to the right to show heavier mass. The camera then pulls back smoothly to show the entire glowing bench — column, ionizer, two-stage analyzer, and fragment spectrum — alive with drifting ions resolving into named peaks and bead sequences.
